narrative:
The model estimates a 90% probability that you will leave your job. In practical terms, that is a very high retention risk, and it is the reason you are currently denied a promotion: the decision is treating likely departure as a reason not to invest further.

The strongest driver was your overall work experience. At 6–10 years, you are more experienced than many employees predicted to stay—about half of them have only 1–5 years—and this profile raised the leaving signal. The second strongest driver was that you have received other job opportunities while in this role; only about one in four employees predicted to stay report this, so it pushed the prediction strongly toward leaving. Third, your 1–5 years with your current organization also leaned toward leaving, suggesting relatively short current tenure and mobility.

These factors pushed the prediction toward “will leave.” To change the outlook, you and your manager should discuss concrete retention levers: career path and promotion timing, recognition, job stability, benefits such as medical insurance, and whether outside opportunities are making this role feel less attractive. The organization should treat this as a retention conversation, not a final judgment.
